claim: RPA is a heterotrimeric protein complex composed of the RPA70, RPA32 and RPA14 subunits.
source: Replication protein A (RPA) is a heterotrimeric protein complex composed of the RPA70, RPA32 and RPA14 subunits (Figure 1A; Fairman and Stillman, 1988; Wood et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fairman and Stillman, 1988 and Wood et al., 1988, and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: RPA is the major eukaryotic single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein.
source: It is the major eukaryotic single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein and has an affinity for ssDNA in the range of 10–9–10–10 M (Blackwell and Borowiec, 1994; Iftode et al., 1999; Kim et al., 1994; Kim et al., 1992; Wold, 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Blackwell and Borowiec, 1994; Iftode et al., 1999; Kim et al., 1994; Kim et al., 1992; Wold, 1997.

claim: RPA has an affinity for ssDNA in the range of 10–9–10–10 M.
source: It is the major eukaryotic single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein and has an affinity for ssDNA in the range of 10–9–10–10 M (Blackwell and Borowiec, 1994; Iftode et al., 1999; Kim et al., 1994; Kim et al., 1992; Wold, 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Blackwell and Borowiec, 1994; Iftode et al., 1999; Kim et al., 1994; Kim et al., 1992; Wold, 1997.

claim: Several DNA-binding domains (DBD-A, B, C, D), also called oligonucleotide binding domains (OB), form the core ssDNA binding region.
source: Several DNA-binding domains (DBD-A, B, C, D), which are also called oligonucleotide binding domains (OB), form the core ssDNA binding region (Figure 1A; Bochkarev et al., 1997; Bochkareva et al., 2002; Fan and Pavletich, 2012; Flynn and Zou, 2010; Murzin, 1993; Yates et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bochkarev et al., 1997; Bochkareva et al., 2002; Fan and Pavletich, 2012; Flynn and Zou, 2010; Murzin, 1993; Yates et al., 2018, and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: RPA is involved in almost all aspects of DNA replication, repair, and recombination.
source: Due to its high affinity for ssDNA, RPA is involved in almost all aspects of DNA replication, repair, and recombination (Caldwell and Spies, 2020; Chen and Wold, 2014; Fanning et al., 2006; Iftode et al., 1999; Maréchal and Zou, 2015; Wold, 1997; Zou et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Caldwell and Spies, 2020; Chen and Wold, 2014; Fanning et al., 2006; Iftode et al., 1999; Maréchal and Zou, 2015; Wold, 1997; Zou et al., 2006.

claim: RPA helps to protect ssDNA from nucleolytic degradation.
source: It helps to protect ssDNA from nucleolytic degradation and prevents ssDNA entanglement by removing DNA secondary structures.
evidence: This is a general statement about RPA function, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: RPA prevents ssDNA entanglement by removing DNA secondary structures.
source: It helps to protect ssDNA from nucleolytic degradation and prevents ssDNA entanglement by removing DNA secondary structures.
evidence: This is a general statement about RPA function, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: RPA serves as a beacon to recruit a plethora of protein factors involved in DNA metabolism, mostly through the RPA70N and RPA32C domains.
source: In addition to its ssDNA binding function, RPA also serves as a beacon to recruit a plethora of protein factors that are involved in DNA metabolism, mostly through the RPA70N and RPA32C (winged-helix) domains (Figure 1A; Awate and Brosh, 2017; Caldwell and Spies, 2020; Fanning et al., 2006; Maréchal and Zou, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Awate and Brosh, 2017; Caldwell and Spies, 2020; Fanning et al., 2006; Maréchal and Zou, 2015, and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: The RPA70N domain adopts an OB fold with a five-stranded anti-parallel beta-barrel.
source: The RPA70N domain adopts an OB fold with a five-stranded anti-parallel beta-barrel but has very weak ssDNA affinity (Figure 1B; Jacobs et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacobs et al., 1999 and referenced in Figure 1B.

claim: RPA70N has very weak ssDNA affinity.
source: The RPA70N domain adopts an OB fold with a five-stranded anti-parallel beta-barrel but has very weak ssDNA affinity (Figure 1B; Jacobs et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacobs et al., 1999 and referenced in Figure 1B.

claim: The primary role of RPA70N is to mediate protein–protein interaction with its basic and hydrophobic groove and a side pocket.
source: Its primary role is to mediate protein–protein interaction with its basic and hydrophobic groove and a side pocket (Figure 1C), as first shown by a series of studies of RPA70N interacting with p53 (Abramova et al., 1997; Dutta et al., 1993; Li and Botchan, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abramova et al., 1997; Dutta et al., 1993; Li and Botchan, 1993, and referenced in Figure 1C.

claim: The groove of RPA70N is flanked by two protruding loops, namely L12 and L45.
source: The groove is flanked by two protruding loops, namely L12 and L45 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Referenced in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The residues forming the groove and the side pocket of RPA70N are highly conserved.
source: The residues forming the groove and the side pocket are highly conserved, indicating that they are critical for RPA70N's protein interaction role (Figure 1D and E; Yariv et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yariv et al., 2023 and referenced in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The conserved residues in RPA70N are critical for RPA70N's protein interaction role.
source: The residues forming the groove and the side pocket are highly conserved, indicating that they are critical for RPA70N's protein interaction role (Figure 1D and E; Yariv et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference based on conservation data, supported by citation to Yariv et al., 2023 and referenced in Figure 1D and E.

claim: In the crystal structure of the RPA70N–p53 complex, the acid-hydrophobic peptide of p53 interacts with the complementary basic and hydrophobic groove, mimicking ssDNA binding to OB domains.
source: In the crystal structure of the RPA70N–p53 complex, the acid-hydrophobic peptide of p53 is shown to interact with the complementary basic and hydrophobic groove, mimicking ssDNA binding to OB domains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Bochkareva et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bochkareva et al., 2005 and referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RPA70N binds to the p53 transactivation domain to coordinate DNA repair with the p53-dependent checkpoint control.
source: RPA70N binds to the p53 transactivation domain to coordinate DNA repair with the p53-dependent checkpoint control (Dutta et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dutta et al., 1993.

claim: RPA70N binds to the N-terminus of ATRIP and is responsible for recruiting the ATR–ATRIP complex to DNA damage sites to initiate the cell-cycle checkpoint.
source: RPA70N also binds to the N-terminus of ATRIP and is responsible for recruiting the ATR–ATRIP complex to DNA damage sites to initiate the cell-cycle checkpoint (Ball et al., 2005; Namiki and Zou, 2006; Zou and Elledge, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ball et al., 2005; Namiki and Zou, 2006; Zou and Elledge, 2003.

claim: RPA70N mediates the interaction of RPA with the MRN complex and the 9-1-1 complex to protect replication forks during the DNA damage response, through binding to MRE11 and RAD9.
source: Later it was shown that RPA70N mediates the interaction of RPA with the MRN complex and the 9-1-1 complex to protect replication forks during the DNA damage response, through binding to MRE11 and RAD9 (Oakley et al., 2009; Olson et al., 2007; Robison et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2008b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oakley et al., 2009; Olson et al., 2007; Robison et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2008b.

claim: ETAA1 is a DNA replication stress response protein and an ATR activator, which interacts with both RPA70N and RPA32C.
source: Recently, studies identified Ewing Tumor-associated Antigen 1 (ETAA1) as a DNA replication stress response protein and an ATR activator, which interacts with both RPA70N and RPA32C (Bass et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2016; Haahr et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bass et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2016; Haahr et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016.

claim: Both BLM (Sgs1) and DNA2 interact with RPA and form a complex to carry out long-range DNA resection during double-strand DNA break repair.
source: Both BLM (Sgs1) and DNA2 interact with RPA and form a complex to carry out long-range DNA resection during double-strand DNA break repair (Cejka et al., 2010; Gravel et al., 2008; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cejka et al., 2010; Gravel et al., 2008; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2008.

claim: RPA was proposed to recruit both DNA2 and BLM through RPA70N, stimulating the helicase activity of BLM while enhancing the nuclease activity of DNA2 by removing DNA secondary structures.
source: RPA was proposed to recruit both DNA2 and BLM through RPA70N, stimulating the helicase activity of BLM while enhancing the nuclease activity of DNA2 by removing DNA secondary structures (Brosh et al., 2000; Doherty et al., 2005; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brosh et al., 2000; Doherty et al., 2005; Nimonkar et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2015.

claim: WRN, HelB and FancJ bind to RPA through RPA70N, and the presence of RPA greatly enhanced their helicase activities.
source: WRN, HelB and FancJ also bind to RPA through RPA70N, and the presence of RPA greatly enhanced their helicase activities (Brosh et al., 1999; Doherty et al., 2005; Guler et al., 2012; Gupta et al., 2007; Hormeno et al., 2022; Shen et al., 1998; Shen et al., 2003; Suhasini et al., 2009; Tkáč et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brosh et al., 1999; Doherty et al., 2005; Guler et al., 2012; Gupta et al., 2007; Hormeno et al., 2022; Shen et al., 1998; Shen et al., 2003; Suhasini et al., 2009; Tkáč et al., 2016.

claim: The RMI1 component of the BTR complex and PrimPol directly associate with RPA70N.
source: For example, the RMI1 component of the BTR complex (BLM–Topo IIIα–RMI1–RMI2) and PrimPol (DNA primase and DNA polymerase) directly associate with RPA70N (Dornreiter et al., 1992; Guilliam et al., 2017; Shorrocks et al., 2021; Wan et al., 2013; Xue et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dornreiter et al., 1992; Guilliam et al., 2017; Shorrocks et al., 2021; Wan et al., 2013; Xue et al., 2013.

claim: Most of the proteins that interact with RPA70N utilize a motif of around 20 amino acids long that contains a mixture of acidic and hydrophobic residues.
source: In general, most of the proteins that interact with RPA70N utilize a motif of around 20 amino acids long that contains a mixture of acidic and hydrophobic residues (Shorrocks et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shorrocks et al., 2021.

claim: The exact sequence of RPA70N-interacting motifs doesn't share much homology, despite the similarity in the overall composition.
source: The exact sequence of these motifs doesn't share much homology, despite the similarity in the overall composition, indicating that each motif might bind to RPA70N differently (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and this is an inference based on sequence analysis.

claim: Each RPA70N-interacting motif might bind to RPA70N differently.
source: The exact sequence of these motifs doesn't share much homology, despite the similarity in the overall composition, indicating that each motif might bind to RPA70N differently (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of sequence homology, referenced in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The authors determined the structures of RPA70N in complex with HelB, BLM, RMI1, WRN, ATRIP, MRE11, RAD9, and ETAA1.
source: To overcome this problem, we fused each target sequence to the C-terminus of RPA70N with a flexible linker. By adjusting the sequence and the linker length of the interacting peptides, we managed to crystalize and determine the structures of RPA70N in complex with HelB, BLM, RMI1, WRN, ATRIP, MRE11, RAD9, and ETAA1 (Figure 1F–N, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–K, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is the primary experimental result of the study, supported by data in Figure 1F–N, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–K, Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: HelB is a conserved helicase that is involved in DNA replication initiation, in replication stress responses and in negatively regulating DNA end-resection.
source: HelB is a conserved helicase that is involved in DNA replication initiation, in replication stress responses and in negatively regulating DNA end-resection (Guler et al., 2012; Hazeslip et al., 2020; Taneja et al., 2002; Tkáč et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guler et al., 2012; Hazeslip et al., 2020; Taneja et al., 2002; Tkáč et al., 2016.

claim: HelB has an RPA-binding motif located in the helicase domain.
source: It has an RPA-binding motif located in the helicase domain and its recruitment to chromatin correlates with the level of RPA (Guler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guler et al., 2012.

claim: HelB recruitment to chromatin correlates with the level of RPA.
source: It has an RPA-binding motif located in the helicase domain and its recruitment to chromatin correlates with the level of RPA (Guler et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guler et al., 2012.

claim: All ssDNA-dependent activities of HelB are greatly stimulated by RPA–ssDNA filaments.
source: A recent in vitro study showed that all ssDNA-dependent activities of HelB are greatly stimulated by RPA–ssDNA filaments (Hormeno et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hormeno et al., 2022.

claim: The RPA70N–HelB complex structure was crystallized in space group P41212 with one molecule in the asymmetry unit.
source: We crystallized a human HelB helicase peptide (HelBp1, residues 496–519) with the human RPA70N (residues 1–120) using the fusion strategy in space group P41212 and found that there is one molecule in the asymmetry unit (Figures 1F and 2B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, referenced in Figures 1F and 2B, Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: In the RPA70N–HelB crystal, the HelB peptide from one fusion protein is bound by a neighboring RPA70N molecule.
source: Crystal packing analysis shows that the HelB peptide from one fusion protein is bound by a neighboring RPA70N molecule (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, referenced in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the 1.6 Å structure of RPA70N–HelB, residues 496–517 of HelB form a four-turn α helix followed by a β turn and a 310 helix.
source: In the 1.6 Å structure, residues 496–517 of HelB form a four-turn α helix followed by a β turn and a 310 helix (Figures 1F and 2B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, referenced in Figures 1F and 2B.

claim: The negatively charged residues E496, E499 and D506 of HelB form hydrogen bonds and salt bridges with RPA70N R81, T60, Q61 and R41.
source: The negatively charged residues E496, E499 and D506 of HelB form hydrogen bonds and salt bridges with RPA70N R81, T60, Q61 and R41 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, referenced in Figure 2B and C.

claim: The hydrophobic residues V500, C504 and F507 of HelB pack against a broad hydrophobic patch formed by RPA70N I83, M97, I95, V93, L87 and M57.
source: The hydrophobic residues V500, C504 and F507 of HelB pack against a broad hydrophobic patch formed by RPA70N I83, M97, I95, V93, L87 and M57 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, referenced in Figure 2C.

claim: W517 of HelB fits into a well-defined pocket (side-pocket) formed by the aliphatic portions of RPA70N N29, R31, R43 and S54.
source: On the left side of the groove, W517 of HelB fits into a well-defined pocket (side-pocket) formed by the aliphatic portions of RPA70N N29, R31, R43 and S54 (Figures 1C, 2D and E).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, referenced in Figures 1C, 2D and E.

claim: The overall binding mode of HelB to RPA70N is similar to that of DNA2.
source: The overall binding mode of HelB to RPA70N is similar to that of DNA2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a comparison based on structural data, referenced in Figure 2F.

claim: Mutation of W517 in HelB to alanine reduced the affinity between HelB peptide and RPA70N from around 4 μM to 16 μM.
source: ITC titration results showed that mutation of W517 in HelB to alanine reduced the affinity between HelB peptide and RPA70N from around 4 μM to 16 μM (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–1D), highlighting the contribution of side-pocket interactions to the overall binding strength.
evidence: This is experimental data from ITC titration, referenced in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–1D.

claim: Further mutation of the hydrophobic residues F507 and C504 in HelB reduced the affinity between RPA70N and HelB by ten fold (37 μM).
source: Further mutation of the hydrophobic residues F507 and C504 in HelB reduced the affinity between RPA70N and HelB by ten fold (37 μM).
evidence: This is experimental data from ITC titration.

claim: In HeLa cells, HelB mutations led to reduced colocalization of HelB–EGFP and endogenous RPA in untreated cells and in camptothecin (CPT) or hydroxyurea (HU) treated cells.
source: In HeLa cells, these mutations led to reduced colocalization of HelB–EGFP and endogenous RPA in untreated cells ls and in camptothecin (CPT) or hydroxyurea (HU) treated cells to different degrees (Figure 2H–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is experimental data from cell-based assays, referenced in Figure 2H–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: HelB-EGFP with C504A/F507A/W517A triple mutation almost completely lost the ability to form obvious RPA foci.
source: HelB-EGFP with C504A/F507A/W517A triple mutation almost completely lost the ability to form obvious RPA foci (Figure 2H–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is experimental data from cell-based assays, referenced in Figure 2H–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Coimmunoprecipitation analysis showed that triple mutant HelB-EGFP pulled down much less RPA than WT.
source: Coimmunoprecipitation (co-IP) analysis also showed that triple mutant HelB-EGFP pulled down much less RPA than WT (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is experimental data from co-IP experiments, referenced in Figure 2K.

claim: Mutation of the conserved arginine residues in RPA70N (R31, R41, R43, R91) significantly reduced the binding of RPA70N to HelBp1.
source: In addition, ITC titration showed that mutation of the conserved arginine esidues in RPA70N (R31, R41, R43, R91) significantly reduced the binding of RPA70N to  HelBp1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This is experimental data from ITC titration, referenced in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–J.

claim: BLM helicase is a multifunctional RecQ family helicase involved in DNA-end resection, restart of stalled replication forks, dissolving Holliday junctions, and processing of ultra-fine DNA bridges.
source: BLM helicase is a multifunctional RecQ family helicase. It is involved in DNA-end resection, restart of stalled replication forks, dissolving Holliday junctions, and processing of ultra-fine DNA bridges (Bythell-Douglas and Deans, 2021; Chu and Hickson, 2009; Croteau et al., 2014; Kitano, 2014; Shorrocks et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bythell-Douglas and Deans, 2021; Chu and Hickson, 2009; Croteau et al., 2014; Kitano, 2014; Shorrocks et al., 2021.

claim: BLM has two RPA70N binding motifs in the N-terminal disordered region, namely residues 146–165 (BLMp1) and residues 550–570 (BLMp2).
source: It has two RPA70N binding motifs in the N-terminal disordered region, namely residues 146–165 (BLMp1) and residues 550–570 (BLMp2) (Figure 3A; Doherty et al., 2005; Shorrocks et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doherty et al., 2005; Shorrocks et al., 2021, and referenced in Figure 3A.

claim: RPA and BLM proteins accumulated along laser lines within 5 min but at relatively low levels.
source: Shorrocks and coworkers reported that RPA and BLM proteins accumulated along laser lines within 5 min but at relatively low levels, RPA microfoci appeared in ~50% of irradiated cells after 15 min as a result of DNA end-resection in S and G2 cells.
evidence: This is a citation to work by Shorrocks et al., 2021.

claim: RPA microfoci appeared in ~50% of irradiated cells after 15 min as a result of DNA end-resection in S and G2 cells.
source: Shorrocks and coworkers reported that RPA and BLM proteins accumulated along laser lines within 5 min but at relatively low levels, RPA microfoci appeared in ~50% of irradiated cells after 15 min as a result of DNA end-resection in S and G2 cells.
evidence: This is a citation to work by Shorrocks et al., 2021.

claim: BLM microfoci appeared at 20 min and co-localized with RPA.
source: Shortly afterwards, at 20 min, BLM microfoci appeared and co-localized with RPA; whereas a BLM mutant lacking both BLMp1 and BLMp2 failed to form microfoci (Shorrocks et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a citation to work by Shorrocks et al., 2021.

claim: A BLM mutant lacking both BLMp1 and BLMp2 failed to form microfoci.
source: Shortly afterwards, at 20 min, BLM microfoci appeared and co-localized with RPA; whereas a BLM mutant lacking both BLMp1 and BLMp2 failed to form microfoci (Shorrocks et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a citation to work by Shorrocks et al., 2021.

claim: In the structure of RPA70N–BLMp2, BLM residues 550–564 are visible and the peptide is bound by two RPA70N molecules.
source: In the structure of RPA70N–BLMp2, BLM residues 550–564 are visible and the peptide is bound by two RPA70N molecules (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, referenced in Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BLMp2 promotes Loop 12 of one RPA70N dimer to interact with α1b of the other RPA70N.
source: Overall, it appears that BLMp2 promotes Loop 12 of one RPA70N dimer to interact with α1b of the other RPA70N, and that each RPA70N provides some of the binding surface for BLMp2 (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data, referenced in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BLMp2 binds to RPA70N with a relatively weak KD of around 18 μM.
source: Using ITC, we found that BLMp2 binds to RPA70N with a relatively weak KD of around 18 μM, and that mutation of BLMp2 residues (D560A, F561A, D562A) almost abolished the binding between BLMp2 and RPA70N (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This is experimental data from ITC titration, referenced in Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Mutation of BLMp2 residues (D560A, F561A, D562A) almost abolished the binding between BLMp2 and RPA70N.
source: Using ITC, we found that BLMp2 binds to RPA70N with a relatively weak KD of around 18 μM, and that mutation of BLMp2 residues (D560A, F561A, D562A) almost abolished the binding between BLMp2 and RPA70N (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D).
evidence: This is experimental data from ITC titration, referenced in Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: In the structure of RPA70N–BLMp1, BLMp1 adopts a kinked conformation and bridges two RPA70N molecules.
source: In the structure of RPA70N–BLMp1, BLMp1 also adopts a kinked conformation and bridges two RPA70N molecules (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study, referenced in Figure 3F.

claim: BLMp1 binds to RPA70N in the reverse direction when compared to BLMp2, HelB or DNA2.
source: However, one major difference is that BLMp1 binds to RPA70N in the reverse direction when compared to BLMp2, HelB or DNA2 (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is a comparison based on structural data, referenced in Figure 1F–H.

claim: The KD of the BLMp1–RPA70N complex is around 16.7 μM, similar to that of the corresponding BLMp2 complex.
source: The KD of the BLMp1–RPA70N complex, as determined by ITC, is around 16.7 μM, similar to that of the corresponding BLMp2 complex (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is experimental data from ITC titration, referenced in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mutation of BLM F160 to alanine greatly reduced the affinity between BLMp1 and RPA70N, resulting in a KD of around 85 μM.
source: Mutation of BLM F160 to alanine greatly reduced the affinity between BLMp1 and RPA70N, resulting in a KD of around 85 μM.
evidence: This is experimental data from ITC titration.

claim: F160A and W154A double mutation reduced the affinity between BLMp1 and RPA70N even more.
source: F160A and W154A double mutation reduced the affinity even more (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is experimental data from ITC titration, referenced in Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: The way that BLMp1 bridges two RPA70N molecules is analogous to the role of the p53 peptide.
source: The two RPA70N molecules are connected by the BLMp1 peptide but do not make other contacts (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H). The way that BLMp1 bridges two RPA70N molecules is analogous to the role of the p53 peptide (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: This is a comparison based on structural data, referenced in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, I and J.

claim: The direction of the BLMp1 peptide in the groove is reversed compared to that of the p53 peptide.
source: However, the direction of the BLMp1 peptide in the groove is reversed compared to that of the p53 peptide (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is a comparison based on structural data, referenced in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J.

claim: In untreated HeLa cells, WT or mutant EGFP–BLM formed few foci.
source: In untreated HeLa cells, WT or mutant EGFP–BLM formed few foci (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is experimental data from cell-based assays, referenced in Figure 3J.

claim: CPT treatment increased the percentage of cells with obvious foci to around 50% for WT and 40% for BLMp1 or BLMp2 mutants.
source: CPT treatment increased the percentage of cells with obvious foci to around 50% for WT and 40% for BLMp1 or BLMp2 mutants (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is experimental data from cell-based assays, referenced in Figure 3K.

claim: The BLMp1 or BLMp2 mutants generally displayed fewer foci per cell when compared to WT.
source: However, the BLMp1 or BLMp2 mutants generally displayed fewer foci per cell when compared to WT (Figure 3J–M).
evidence: This is experimental data from cell-based assays, referenced in Figure 3J–M.

claim: The BLMp1 and BLMp2 dual mutant formed far fewer foci, even after CPT treatment.
source: The BLMp1 and BLMp2 dual mutant formed far fewer foci, even after CPT treatment (Figure 3J–M).
evidence: This is experimental data from cell-based assays, referenced in Figure 3J–M.

claim: Mutating the RPA70N interacting residues in BLM reduced its binding to RPA.
source: Co-IP experiments showed that mutating the RPA70N interacting residues in BLM reduced its binding to RPA (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is experimental data from co-IP experiments, referenced in Figure 3N.

claim: Mutation of the conserved arginine residues in RPA70N (R31, R41, R43, R91) significantly reduced the binding of RPA70N to BLMp2 and BLMp1.
source: Not surprisingly, mutation of the conserved arginine residues in RPA70N (R31, R41, R43, R91) significantly reduced the binding of RPA70N to BLMp2 and BLMp1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–I).
evidence: This is experimental data from ITC titration, referenced in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–I.

claim: RMI1 is a subunit in the BTR complex and mainly mediates protein–protein interaction.
source: RMI1 is another RPA partner. It is a subunit in the BTR complex and mainly mediates protein–protein interaction (Shorrocks et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2008a; Xue et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shorrocks et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2008a; Xue et al., 2013.

claim: The RPA70N interaction motif of RMI1 is located between its two OB folds.
source: The RPA70N interaction motif is located between its two OB folds (Figure 4A).
evidence: Referenced in Figure 4A.

claim: In the RPA70N–RMI1 complex structure, RMI1 residues 243-259 form two short α helixes with a β turn in the middle.
source: In the RPA70N–RMI1 complex structure, RMI1 residues 243-259 form two short α helixes with a β turn in the middle (Figures 4B and 1I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

source: Of particular interest is that many of the partner peptides appear to be able to connect two RPA70N domains (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is an observation from structural data, referenced in Figure 10A.

claim: Some RPA70N-interacting proteins (BTR complex, WRN, ATRIP, p53 and ETAA1) are themselves often dimers or oligomers.
source: Intriguingly, some of these partner proteins (BTR complex, WRN, ATRIP, p53 and ETAA1) are themselves often dimers or oligomers (Cho et al., 1994; Compton et al., 2008; Deshpande et al., 2017; Hodson et al., 2022; Thada and Cortez, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cho et al., 1994; Compton et al., 2008; Deshpande et al., 2017; Hodson et al., 2022; Thada and Cortez, 2021.

claim: RPA is able to recruit ATR/ATRIP to stalled replication forks, which nucleates many RPA70N-interacting DNA damage response proteins.
source: For example, RPA is able to recruit ATR/ATRIP to stalled replication forks, which nucleates many RPA70N-interacting DNA damage response proteins (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A; Bass et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2016; Haahr et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016; Maréchal and Zou, 2015; Saldivar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bass et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2016; Haahr et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2016; Maréchal and Zou, 2015; Saldivar et al., 2017, and referenced in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Frattini et al., 2021 proposed the formation of a nucleation complex including RPA–ssDNA, ATR/ATRIP, TopBP1, MRN and the 9-1-1 complex, which stabilizes TopBP1 at stalled replication forks.
source: Frattini et al., 2021 proposed the formation of a nucleation complex including RPA–ssDNA, ATR/ATRIP, TopBP1, MRN and the 9-1-1 complex, which stabilizes TopBP1 at stalled replication forks.

claim: TopBp1 condensates to dynamic higher-order assemblies by multivalent cooperative interactions to achieve robust ATR activation and signal amplification.

evidence: This is a citation to work by Frattini et al., 2021.

claim: One RPA usually covers around 30 nt ssDNA.
source: One RPA usually covers around 30 nt ssDNA (Kim et al., 1994); for medium to long ssDNA, there are multiple copies of bound RPA.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 1994.

claim: The bridge-forming nature of some of the partner peptides in combination with many RPAs on ssDNA could greatly enhance the efficiency of partner recruitment when needed for DNA damage response.
source: The bridge-forming nature of some of the partner peptides in combination with many RPAs on ssDNA could greatly enhance the efficiency of partner recruitment when needed for DNA damage response (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural findings, referenced in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Under normal conditions, RPA molecules are not clustered on ssDNA and have a relatively weak affinity for many DNA damage response proteins.
source: Under normal conditions, RPA molecules are not clustered on ssDNA and have a relatively weak affinity for many DNA damage response proteins, as shown by the dissociation constant values measured in this study and previous studies (Hegnauer et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2018; Souza-Fagundes et al., 2012; Yeom et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from this study and citations to Hegnauer et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2018; Souza-Fagundes et al., 2012; Yeom et al., 2019.

claim: Upon DNA damage, RPAs nucleate on exposed ssDNA quickly, owing to their sub-nanomolar affinity for ssDNA, and recruit corresponding proteins.
source: Upon DNA damage, RPAs nucleate on exposed ssDNA quickly, owing to their sub-nanomolar affinity for ssDNA, and recruit corresponding proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge and the findings of the study.

claim: With sufficient copies of RPA bound to ssDNA, the weak affinity of monomeric RPA70N toward target protein is now overwhelmed by multiple interaction interfaces.
source: With sufficient copies of RPA bound to ssDNA, the weak affinity of monomeric RPA70N toward target protein is now overwhelmed by multiple interaction interfaces (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural findings, referenced in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: RPA has a strong propensity to assemble into dynamic condensates (undergo phase separation), which is likely to be driven by RPA2 and could be stimulated by ssDNA binding.
source: A recent study showed that RPA has a strong propensity to assemble into dynamic condensates (undergo phase separation), which is likely to be driven by RPA2 and could be stimulated by ssDNA binding (Spegg et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a citation to work by Spegg et al., 2023.

claim: RPA condensation enhances interactions with the BTR complex.
source: More importantly, the data demonstrate that RPA condensation enhances interactions with the BTR complex.
evidence: This is a citation to work by Spegg et al., 2023.

claim: The multivalent interactions observed in the crystal structures could contribute significantly to condensation-driven DNA damage response processes.
source: The multivalent interactions that we observed in the crystal structures could contribute significantly to these condensation-driven DNA damage response processes (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is speculation based on structural findings, referenced in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: In imaging analysis, HelB, BLM, WRN, ATRIP and ETAA1 formed a substantial number of foci and colocalized with endogenous RPA, and this colocalization was further stimulated by CPT or HU treatment.

evidence: This is experimental data from cell-based assays, referenced in Figure 2H-J, Figure 3J-M, Figure 5H-K, Figure 6F-J, Figure 9D-G.

claim: Mutation of interface residues significantly weakened the formation of foci and colocalization.
source: Mutation of interface residues significantly weakened the formation of foci and colocalization (Figure 2H-J, Figure 3J-M, Figure 5H-K, Figure 6F-J, Figure 9D-G).
evidence: This is experimental data from cell-based assays, referenced in Figure 2H-J, Figure 3J-M, Figure 5H-K, Figure 6F-J, Figure 9D-G.
